newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Agency plans first aid shipment for Albania's poor.
newsitem.headline: Agency plans first aid shipment for Albania's poor.

text.p: The U.N. World Food Programme (WFP) geared up to unload the biggest food aid shipment to Albania since the launch of a multinational security mission to the chaotic Balkan state, officials said.

A Reuters Television producer at the main port of Durres said a ship bringing more than 400 tonnes of wheat flour, beans and vegetable oil arrived on Tuesday. Aid officials said it was expected to start unloading to a nearby warehouse on Wednesday.
Asked when deliveries of food aid to Albania's poor would start, Jean-Marie Boucher, head of the WFP Albania mission, told reporters in Durres: "It could be Wednesday or Thursday."
He said WFP, the world's biggest food aid agency, was discussing a strategy to distribute the aid in cooperation with the Italian-led multinational force.
"We are not going to distribute food in unsafe areas without a military escort," WFP spokeswoman Laura Boldrini told Reuters by telephone from Rome.

Nearly 1,200 Italian, French and Spanish soldiers belonging to the eight-nation U.N.-backed force arrived by land and sea in Albania on Tuesday at the start of a mission to protect delivery of emergency food aid and medicines to the country's poor.
Albania slid into near-anarchy earlier this year after the failure of fraudulent investment plans in which many had invested their life savings.
Nearly 300 people have been killed in the armed uprising after people looted armouries deserted by soldiers and police.

In Durres, 40 km (25 miles) west of Tirana, Boucher estimated that the relief effort would last for a few months. The aid is aimed at hospitals, orphanages, homes for the handicapped and elderly and destitute families across Albania.
"As this is not a famine, we are acting as a bridge until things return to normal," he said.
Albania's poor desperately need food. Basic food costs have shot up, social security payments have stopped and state food supplies are not reaching institutions, aid officials said.

Relief agencies estimate that one in 10 Albanians needs humanitarian aid. The Geneva-based International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), which does not rely on armed escorts, has been distributing food and medicines since last month.
The Albanian government warmly welcomed the arrival of the soldiers on Tuesday and said they could help restore order.
U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan applauded the start of "Operation Alba", but said the soldiers should leave the disarming of rebels to the Albanian authorities.
"This operation is a humanitarian one to make sure aid gets to the people," he said in Rome.
Albania said on Tuesday it wanted to meet donors and international investors as soon as possible to try to kick-start its economy, which has been throttled by the violence.
Finance Minister Arben Malaj said he had had recent meetings with the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank.

"We have it confirmed from Italy that it will invite donors, possible donors and others to an international conference," he told the annual meeting of the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development in London. He gave no date.
There were no signs on Tuesday of an end to the violence in Albania. Police killed an escaped convict in a shoot-out in the south-eastern town of Bilisht after he wounded two officers.
Police in Gramsh, 100 km (60 miles) south of Tirana, confiscated three trucks full of automatic rifles, machine guns and grenade launchers in a raid, Albania's news agency ATA said.
Gramsh has been a centre for the illegal arms trade after three army depots nearby were emptied and 100,000 Kalashnikov assault rifles were stolen.
